projectOutComesReport:
In this project, we measured how rocks, which were originally formed at great depth, were brought to the surface where they sit today, using a technique called thermochronology. Through a combination of laboratory analyses and computation, this technique allows us to study the time-temperature path that these rocks have followed (i.e., what temperature they were at at what time in the past). Since temperature increases with depth underground, this in turn allows us to estimate how deeply buried these rocks were in the past, and when they were brought closer to the surface through erosion. In many cases, we found that rocks from the North American continent were brought to the surface relatively rapidly during a time period known as the Cryogenian, between 720 and 635 million years ago. For much of this period, Earth's climate is thought to have been in a "Snowball Earth" state, where the oceans freeze down to the equator and all continents were covered by Antarctica-like ice sheets. If rocks were brought to the surface during this interval, glacial erosion likely played a role. To better understand this signal, we compared the time-temperature paths of rocks from different locations across North America, from the continental margins to the interior. Tectonic processes play a larger role in erosion along continental margins (near plate boundaries), therefore, if this erosion was largely a result of tectonics, we expect it to only occur at the margin, while if glacial erosion was the cause we expect both heterogeneous ("hit-or-miss") erosion along the margins as well as more even, deep erosion in the interior. Our results suggest significant erosion in many continental interior locations, and more heterogeneous erosion both at North American margins and at zones of crustal weakness in the interior where tectonic stresses may cause local uplift or subsidence. These results support the hypothesis that Cryogenian glacial erosion may have contributed to a feature known as the Great Unconformity, where many sedimentary rocks are missing from the rock record due to erosion. Further results involving the pattern of exhumation (uplift due to erosion) across the Canadian Shield suggest that this episode of erosion may have eroded and fragmented what may have once been an originally continuous basin of sedimentary rocks from the Paleoproterozoic (between 2.5 and 1.6 billion years ago), leaving now only discontinuous remnants.

Other major outcomes beyond these scientific results included the development of the first fully open-source time-Temperature (t-T) inversion software, Thermochron.jl as well as the open-sourcing of a range of new and existing thermochronology software under the OpenThermochronology organization, which we initiated as part of this project. In addition, we note that this project supported the postdoctoral research and professional development of a first-generation college student.

abstractText:
To understand how the brain functions and cure brain disorders, neuroscientists and clinicians need brain mapping devices.  This project will develop the next generation of stretchable and transparent electrode arrays with unprecedented scale and resolution for brain recording and stimulation. This program will not only generate broad impacts in neuroscience through proactive device translation efforts in and beyond this project, but also create unique opportunities for novel neuroprosthetics. Through generating neural interfaces that will allow human-like performance in neuroprosthetic limbs and retinal prostheses with chronic biocompatibility, this program will impact more than 3 million people in the U.S. who live with upper limb loss, paralysis due to tetraplegia, blindness due to retinitis pigmentosa, or epilepsy. The proposed multidisciplinary educational/outreach program will engage hundreds of students through research experiences for underrepresented K-12 students, active undergraduate research involvements, graduate leadership training in device translation, and augmented engineering curricula.

The research objective of this project is to investigate a set of foundational materials and device problems to for the first time establish a new unique device technology "multifunctional nanomesh microelectrodes" to shift the current paradigm of neural interface from rigid, opaque neuroelectrode arrays towards ultrasoft and transparent ones.  Stretchable and transparent neuroelectrode arrays are two emerging neural interfaces due to their chronic biocompatibility and multimodal compatibility, respectively. However, both systems are currently confounded by their scalability since fundamentally, no existing electrode materials can simultaneously provide the required system-level properties of electrochemical interfaces, electrical conductance, and chronic biocompatibility in addition to the mandatory mechanical stretchability or optical transparency. Based on strong preliminary results, the PI hypothesizes that multifunctional nanomesh microelectrodes can possess an unprecedented combination of all functionalities needed for this aforementioned paradigm shift including low impedance, large stretchability, high transparency, and chronic biocompatibility. This project will holistically test this hypothesis through innovative theoretical design, experimental realization, and system demonstration/validation, and proactively integrate closed-loop device translation and experiential education activities.  Vertically, the unprecedented combination of large throughput, chronic biocompatibility and multimodal compatibility of the resulting neural interface device will yield profound impacts to both our studying of complex networks in the central nervous system and interfacing with the brain. Laterally, the multifunctional-nanomesh device concept, theoretical framework, and fabrication knowledge can also be transformative in many other fields such as optoelectronics, energy storage, and nanogenerators if stretchability and/or transparency are desired.

projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: This project advanced the scientific foundations and technological capabilities of soft, multimodal bioelectronic materials and devices capable of chronic, high-fidelity integration with neural and physiological systems. The core innovation lay in developing a new class of flexible, stretchable neuroelectronic platforms that combined multimodal sensing-including electrical, mechanical, and electrochemical modalities-into a single, biocompatible material system. Over the life of the project, our team produced 10 peer-reviewed publications (including Advanced Materials, Nature Communications, and Biosensors and Bioelectronics), delivered 18 invited talks, and filed 3 patent disclosures. These outcomes significantly advance the state of the art in soft neuroelectronics, behavioral neuroscience tools, and multimodal physiological sensing. Key research highlights include: (1) Development of Nanomesh-Based Neural Interfaces: We engineered elastic, nanomesh electronics that provide cellular-resolution interfacing with the brain surface and studied their structure-property relationship. These devices exhibited submicron-level feature uniformity, mechanical properties that match cortical tissue, and robust signal quality for chronic recording. This work represents a step forward in conformal neural interface technology. (2) Electrochemical Uniformity in PEDOT:PSS Coating: We demonstrated an array-wide uniform potentiostatic deposition of PEDOT:PSS on multichannel microelectrodes, ensuring consistent impedance reduction across high-density electrode arrays. This method offers scalable and reliable performance for electrical recording and stimulation. (3) Mechanistic Study of Neural Probe Insertion: We investigated failure modes in soft probe insertion into brain-like hydrogels and identified critical thresholds for buckling, fracture, and tip deformation. This insight has direct implications for minimizing surgical damage. And (4) Crosstalk in Polymer Microelectrode Arrays: We performed a seminal analysis of the crosstalk between two adjacent polymer microelectrodes experimentally and through modeling. In addition to standardizing neural electrode array crosstalk characterization, this study not only reveals the dependence of the crosstalk in polymer microelectrode arrays on a variety of key device parameters but also provides general guidelines for the design of thin polymer microelectrode arrays for high-quality neural signal recording.

Broader Impacts: This project has important translational and societal implications. By developing soft and multimodal bioelectronic systems, we contribute to next-generation brain-computer interfaces, neurotherapeutic platforms, and continuous health monitoring technologies. These innovations are foundational to fundamental neuroscience, personalized medicine, and closed-loop neuroprosthetic interventions. Our education and training activities spanned high school through postdoctoral levels. This highly interdisciplinary project has particularly provided comprehensive training for students. Significantly, six Ph.D. students in the PI's group were supported by this project, and to date, three have graduated. They received interdisciplinary training in electrode array design, microfabrication, electrochemistry, materials and device characterization, and neural engineering. After graduation, one student joined a neurotechnology start-up in California, while two students became postdoctoral research fellows in the U.S., continuing in the neural device field. PI Fang also incorporated some fundamental knowledge from this project and recent breakthroughs in neuroelectronics in his teaching. In particular, the PI has transformed his previous materials and device training and recent neural engineering application practice into the development of a new graduate-level course at Dartmouth, ENGS 127 Bioelectronics, which introduces the fundamentals and applications of micro-and nano-technology-based bioelectronics. Finally, the nanomesh electrode arrays developed in this project are now enabling new investigations in collaborating labs, for instance, to discover neuronal firing patterns underlying anesthetic-induced slow waves. In summary, this project not only produced cutting-edge technological advances in brain-interfacing materials and devices but also created bioelectronic educational pipelines and translational pathways that will have long-term impacts on both scientific and societal levels.

abstractText:
Non-technical description: Stretchable electronics have emerged as promising platforms for many important areas such as bio-mimetics, health monitoring, biomedical therapeutics, and soft robotics. This project investigates a set of foundational materials science problems to, for the first time, establish a new electronic materials platform - Si nanomeshes - for next-generation stretchable electronics. The transformative aspect of this project arises from the broad utility of the resulting design and engineering knowledge for nanomesh electronic materials, having profound impacts to not only fundamental materials science but also a broad range of applications in human-electronic interfaces and smart robots. The collaborative team also utilizes this project to integrate creative educational activities with cutting-edge research at multiple levels through: (1) engaging K-12 students via summer research and exhibiting at Oklahoma WONDERtorium Children's museum; (2) actively attracting undergraduate students for early research; and (3) the continuous curriculum development at both Northeastern University and Oklahoma State University to expand capacity in the soft electronic materials field. 

Technical description: Stretchable electronics research has long been facing the dichotomy between device performance and density. In the past decade, there has been significant progress in realizing stretchable semiconductors, however, existing approaches are still incomplete when high-density, high-performance stretchable electronics are needed. On the basis of strong preliminary results from the research team, the principal investigators hypothesize that with tailored nanomesh geometries and engineered sidewall surface states, Si nanomeshes can achieve simultaneously large stretchability, high mobility and high reliability that are needed for high-density stretchable electronics. Through both theoretical and experimental investigations, this project aims to investigate and establish the interrelationship of structure-processing-properties of Si nanomeshes for stretchable devices. Key structure variables to investigate include in-plane nanomesh pattern, out-of-plane materials stacking and sidewall surface states, while main properties targeted are mechanical flexibility, stretchability, and carrier transport mobilities. The project then achieves Si nanomeshes with desired mesh patterns through viable top-down approaches, prints and fabricates sidewall engineered Si-nanomesh based stretchable devices. A set of combined optical and electrical characterizations systematically investigate the properties of sidewall-engineered Si nanomeshes under stretching and scaling. Besides potential applications for high-performance stretchable electronics, this semiconductor nanomesh concept provides a new platform for materials engineering, and is expected to yield a new family of stretchable materials having tunable electronic and optoelectronic properties with customized nanostructures.

projectOutComesReport:
This project aims to, for the first time, establish a new unique electronic materials paradigm - Silicon (Si) nanomesh - for next-generation stretchable electronics. Over the past three years, we have successfully fabricated Si nanomesh using the Indium grain boundary lithography method and transfer printed them onto thin polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) substrate (npj Flexible Electronics, 3, Article number: 9, 2019). By making a silicon film into homogeneous nanomesh with spring-like nano traces, we demonstrated a high electron mobility of 50 cm2/V.s, and moderate stretchability with a one-time strain of 25% and cyclic strain of 14% after stretching for 1000 cycles, further improvable with optimized nanomesh designs. 

We have also studied the mechanical properties of three types of regular-shape nanomesh by analytical models that are validated by finite element analysis (FEA) results (Journal of Applied Mechanics, 87(10): 101010, 2020). The results showed that for the same level of material density, the hexagonal nanomesh exhibit isotropic eﬀective modulus and stretchability that are useful in a variety of applications. Our preliminary results also showed that for sinusoidal or partial-circular arc traces, there exists an amplitude-period ratio that gives optimum mechanical stretchability, and the rigidity is governed by the width of the traces. PI Wang's group is writing the manuscript for a journal article on the mechanical properties of nanomesh structures with various curvy traces.

Finally, we have successfully fabricated nanomesh-based devices on PDMS with total device thickness down to only 10μm (IEEE IEDM 2022, accepted). Ultrathin PDMS offers excellent potential as a substrate material for soft electronics applications, including softness, transparency, and conformability.

This project has involved and trained several Ph.D. students, master's students and undergraduate trainees. In particular, the lead student of this project in PI Fang's group, Kyung Jin Seo, has successfully defended his Ph.D. thesis and recently joined Science Corp, a start-up company for brain interface as the materials & microfabrication engineer. One Ph.D. student and two master's students in PI Wang's group at Oklahoma State University (OSU) led the efforts in developing fundamental mechanics theories: Sandra Vinnikova has completed all the research tasks and will defend her thesis in Spring 2023; Oishwarya Bhowmik graduated with her master's degree and joined Pennsylvania State University to pursue her Ph.D. degree; Rakib Rahman also graduated with a master's degree and continued his Ph.D. study at PI Wang's group. This research also promoted the careers of the PIs Fang and Wang, who were both promoted to associate professors with tenure at their respective institution. The knowledge from this project has enriched STEM curriculums, such as ENGS 135 Thin Films and Microfabrication Technology, taught by PI Fang at Dartmouth College, and MAE 4363 Advanced Methods in Design, taught by PI Wang at OSU.

abstractText:
Dark matter composes 85% of the matter in the universe. Understanding the properties of this unknown matter sets the stage for many important advances for humankind as well as understanding the universe.  Dark matter gathers significantly around objects with strong gravitational fields, i.e. black holes and very massive stars.  Recent advances in gravitational wave and radio astronomy have allowed unprecedented glimpses into black holes and very massive stars.  The proposed project computes the interactions between dark matter, gravitational and electromagnetic waves in the environment surrounding black holes and very massive stars.  These calculations, combined with state-of-the-art numerical simulations, are designed to provide a variety of telltale signatures of dark matter.  The PI and a trainee will travel to the Joint Institute for Laboratory Astrophysics (JILA) to implement these numerical simulations.  The resulting work product seeks to turn black holes and very massive stars into dark matter detectors.  Broader impacts of this work include engaging local high-school students and the greater New Hampshire-Vermont community to understand developments in dark matter (particle physics) research.  In addition, the PI will also promote the inclusion of underrepresented groups in STEM fields, e.g., through giving lectures at Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs).  Finally, the trainee supported by this award will be exposed to advanced general relativity, quantum field theory, and numerical techniques used to simulate the environments surrounding black holes and compact stars.

Dark matter congregates significantly around objects with large gravitational fields such as black holes and compact stars.  For this project, the PI considers electromagnetic and gravitational wave signatures of bosonic (axion) dark matter from these compact objects. Using effective field theory techniques, the PI includes the most important interactions in order to properly understand the evolution of this dark matter.  The large gravitational fields introduce a new scale, the Schwarzschild radius, which alters the dark matter oscillations into gravitational and electromagnetic waves.  This effect is analogous to the Mikheyev-Smirnov-Wolfenstein effect for neutrinos.  These alterations affect both superradiant and non-superradiant enhanced processes.   The PI and a trainee will travel to the Joint Institute for Laboratory Astrophysics (JILA) to vet the new, unique dark matter signatures with well-vetted numerical simulations of the astrophysical backgrounds in order to determine their efficacy in producing statistically significant probes of dark matter.  By leveraging multi-wavelength astronomy, very-long-baseline interferometry (such as the Event Horizon Telescope) as well as the current (and near future) capabilities of gravitational wave astronomy, the fellowship goal is to generate viable search strategies to identify regions of parameter space for bosonic (axion) dark matter.

projectOutComesReport:
One of humanity’s most profound questions concerns the nature and evolution of the universe. At the heart of this lies dark matter—a mysterious substance that comprises roughly 85 percent of all matter in the cosmos.  Only about 15 percent of the universe’s matter is “ordinary” matter —the material that forms stars, planets, and living beings like you and me.  This matter dominantly interacts with ordinary matter gravitationally.  Identifying and characterizing this unseen matter is crucial, because its dominance over the cosmos has profound implications for our understanding of physics, the evolution of the universe, and the remarkable technologies humanity can develop.

Beyond the mystery of dark matter, the first detection of gravitational waves in 2015 opened an entirely new window on the cosmos. For the first time in history humanity can explore the universe through ripples in spacetime itself. Traditional telescopes are now complemented by gravitational‑wave observatories, together delivering a richer, multi-dimensional picture of the Universe’s composition.

This project unites two frontier topics: the nature of dark matter and the emerging field of gravitational wave astronomy.  We determined the conditions under which electromagnetic radiation can convert into gravitational waves (and vice-versa).  In addition, we described how certain dark‑matter candidates can convert into photons.  By exploiting these conversion processes we open novel pathways for probing dark matter, while also providing complementary tools that enhance traditional electromagnetic observations with gravitational wave data.

abstractText:
Non-Technical Summary:

With support from the Solid State and Materials Chemistry and Condensed Matter Physics Programs in the Division of Materials Research, this research examines the effect that tiny amounts of light-sensitive inclusions, such as small molecules, (i.e., switchable dopants) have on the long-range helical structure, and hence, photophysical properties of liquid-crystals (LCs – the same type of material found in Liquid Crystal Display (LCD) televisions). The Aprahamian group studies the fundamental factors that govern the interactions between the switchable dopant and host LC to gain insights into how to better control such phenomena. The aim of the project is to understand if this strategy can be used in programming the optical properties of the LCs. This knowledge in turn advances applications ranging from active smart surfaces, to sensors, color filters, and responsive reflectors. Aprahamian and his group also participate in educational and outreach activities that i) engage high-school and undergraduate students from different educational levels and backgrounds in research, and ii) increase public knowledge and appreciation of important chemical concepts. For example, the PI’s group uses interactive demonstrations to explain to the public how fluorophores work. The group’s public outreach and participation in STEM-related events, such as the Dartmouth Science Day, help disseminate the group’s work to broad audiences.  

Technical Summary: 
Adaptive liquid crystals (LCs) are used in a myriad of applications ranging from active smart surfaces to sensors, color filters, and responsive reflectors. Chiral switchable dopants are usually at the heart of these applications, though the nature of the interactions between them and the host LC, and how these interactions control the self-assembly and helical twist of the chiral LC, which are responsible for the LC’s photophysical properties, is poorly understood. With the help of this grant from the Solid State and Materials Chemistry and Condensed Matter Physics Programs in the Division of Materials Research the Aprahamian group conducts structure-property analyses to develop an understanding of the intermolecular interactions and structural parameters that control both the helical twisting power (i.e., the ability of a chiral dopant to twist a nematic phase) and the change in helical twisting power upon switching of chiral photochromic dopants (i.e., hydrazones). The group also uses the bistable hydrazone photoswitches to kinetically trap the self-assembly of the LCs, and hence, the colors reflected from their surfaces. Overall, this research enhances the toolbox and capabilities available to practitioners, thus allowing for the realization of the numerous applications that adaptive LC materials are slated for.  Additionally, Aprahamian and his group are involved in outreach activities that strengthen and extend the group's informal and formal science education partnerships and networks with local schools and science museums.

projectOutComesReport:
The project "Kinetically Trapping the Self-Assembly and Photophysical Properties of Liquid Crystals" was focused on developing photoswitchable chiral dopants that can effectively control the helical self-assembly of liquid crystals (LCs), and hence their ability to reflect different wavelengths of light. For example, we performed structure/property analysis on more than twenty derivatives of isosorbide linked hydrazone switches to understand how the connectivity between these two units, and the nature of the groups on the hydrazone effect the ability of the dopants to result in large b values (i.e., efficient chiral information transfer) in LCs, and change in the value upon photoisomerization (Db). We found out that dispersion interactions, structural similarity with the host LC, and the dihedral angle of the hydrazone in its E form are among the important factors that result in high b values. We then took advantage of the insights to design dopants that reflect visible light and used them in engineering low-energy consuming reversible multicolor LC displays. As part of these studies, we discovered multistate dopants (i.e., ones that have four different, stable and addressable isomers) that result in an unusual phase change from cholesteric to focal conic and used this property in a steganography application. We also developed triptycene as a new chiral unit for such applications and showed that it can result in high b values as well. Structure property analysis, including the use of azobenzene switches for comparison, helped us glean deeper into the structural motifs and trends that result in efficient chiral information transfer to the LC. These dopants were then used in designing reusable LC canvases that can be activated with light/light or light/heat stimuli. Lastly, we developed a new approach to controlling the color reflected from LC elastomer surfaces. To this end we crosslinked the elastomers with hydrazone switches and applied the geometry change the latter undergo upon photoisomerization to contract and expand the pitch of the elastomer, and hence their color reflection.  

The broader impact of this project lies in developing a better understanding of how chiral information transfer occurs from switchable dopants to LC hosts, and how to tap into this effect in designing reversible, multi-color LC canvases. Using structure property analysis, we also gained a better understanding of how to design better chiral dopants, that results in visible color reflection. Moreover, we introduced triptycene as an effective chiral unit in such applications. Finally, we showed a new method for tuning the reflected colors from LC elastomer surfaces, by crosslinking them with hydrazone switches, and using light switching to contract/expand the pitch of the elastomer.

Significantly, the most important impact of this grant was the training of graduate and postdoctoral students, who came from different backgrounds, in liquid crystal, supramolecular, organic and materials chemistry, in addition to various characterization techniques. This training equipped the students for positions in industry and academia. Moreover, this grant enabled us to interact with the general public through our numerous outreach events, which broadened the reach of the science we are conducting in the laboratory.

abstractText:
In this project, two questions are investigated: first, how financial difficulties were distributed within low-income communities before and during the COVID-19 pandemic and, second, the extent to which social welfare decisions mitigated or exacerbated debt burdens and which of these decisions were most (or least) successful in protecting low-income families from serious financial difficulties.  When faced with economic insecurity, many Americans take on debt.  Although access to credit can provide families a resource in times of crisis, debt is often burdensome to repay for low-income families, and can exacerbate, rather than relieve, economic strain and insecurity.   With the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, many Americans faced sudden and new sources of economic insecurity, and official responses to the pandemic were diverse. This study contributes to understanding the combined effects of debt and official responses in low-income communities when a crisis strikes.  One important goal of this project is to inform decision-makers about low-income debt and economic insecurity during the COVID-19 crisis in order to increase the effectiveness of future interventions. 

The research questions are addressed through linkages of consumer credit, alternative financial services, and state data sets.  Levels of indebtedness in low-income communities are captured with zip-code level quarterly data on consumer credit, such as mortgages and credit cards.  Alternative financial service use—e.g., payday and title loans—is obtained from Q1 2019 through Q4 2020.  These data are linked to state and zip-level data that include sociodemographic characteristics, COVID-related constraints, and state-level social safety net procedures.  Analysis involves, first, description of debt patterns in vulnerable communities in the United States before and after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Second, a variety of statistical models are used to investigate associations between debt problems and official responses to the pandemic in these communities.

jrnl.artTitl: Inequality in high-cost borrowing and unemployment insurance generosity in US states during the COVID-19 pandemic
jrnl.auth: Berger, Lawrence M and Brown, Meta and Collins, J Michael and Dwyer, Rachel E and Houle, Jason N and Moulton, Stephanie and Norris, Davon and Rhodes, Alec P

orgLongName: Directorate for Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences
orgLongName2: Division of Social and Economic Sciences
perfAddress: 20 N Main St, Blunt Hall, Room 3
program: COVID-19 Research, EXP PROG TO STIM COMP RES
projectOutComesReport:
Our project accomplished three principle aims. First, we constructed a nationally representative data system using consumer credit, alternative financial services, and state policy data to quantify levels of indebtedness from mainstream (e.g., credit cards) and alternative (e.g., payday loans) credit instruments in low-income communities across US states prior to and in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. We construct a state-level dataset with detailed measures of social welfare policy, policies related to COVID-19 response, and state economic and population characteristics. We linked individual-level and zip-code level credit report and alternative financial services data to the state dataset. Second, we inventoried debt problems among communities in the United States in consumer credit and alternative financial services data and tracked patterns of debt before and after the onset of the COVID-19 crisis across US states. We analyzed trends in levels and types of debt over time across income levels among American populations across place (zip/state). Our measures of debt problems include access to credit, the cost of credit, and challenges with debt repayment and collections. Third, in several specific papers, we estimated associations of the COVID-19 pandemic with debt problems in American communities and social welfare program generosity and accessibility.

Broadly, one of the most important contributions of the project is to extend our understanding of alternative financial service uses in the online market. Previous scientific research has examined how inequality and segregation are linked with “brick and mortar” alternative financial service use (e.g., the presence of payday loan and title loan storefronts). Broadly, this literature suggests that segregation and inequality shape access to financial services and use of alternative financial services primarily because AFS is more prevalent and available in disadvantaged areas. However, the majority of alternative financial service use now operates through online lenders, not through storefronts. With our data, we are able to examine these online lenders, and we find that segregation and inequality are associated with online use of AFS. This suggests that segregation and inequality are important determinants of AFS use not only because of the supply of credit in these areas (storefronts), but also due to the demand or need for credit among residents of these areas.

Moreover, our results demonstrates that more generous social welfare benefits (vis a vis unemployment insurance in one article and the social safety net for low-income populations in another article) may reduce the use of and need for high cost credit, and that these effects were particularly strong during the COVID-19 pandemic, a time during which UI generosity was historically high. The basic premise of this hypothesis is that social safety nets reduce economic risk for families and households, and therefore when social safety nets contract, households need to borrow more (and often at high cost) to make ends meet. That we find larger associations between UI generosity and AFS outcomes during the COVID pandemic, suggests that substantial increases in funding to UI (and perhaps other social safety net programs) can protect households from high-cost borrowing. Our paper on the social safety and unsecured credit use builds on these other contributions. By examining alternative forms of credit, we see evidence that more generous safety nets increase access and use of more traditional forms of credit such as credit cards, while decreasing use of the highest cost alternative financial services loans including payday loans. We argue that more generous safety nets thus foster credit market inclusion because supported populations both have more access to traditional instruments and have sufficient security about repayment to be able to use just as do more advantaged Americans.

 

Our findings also have important implications for the regulation and monitoring of emerging credit markets, particularly online credit markets. Our work also identifies issues in financial coping for American populations that will inform policy and related efforts to better target social support to those populations. For example, our findings highlight different outcomes for communities in restrictive versus permissive state credit environments which may have far-reaching implications for pathways towards economic opportunity. In addition, our findings have implications for state governments and their budgeting priorities for funding UI and other social safety net programs. If such programs have the potential to reduce economic vulnerability and increase well-being (our results suggest they do), then increasing the generosity of such programs may generate positive externalities among the state’s citizenry.

 

Finally, our work highlights the importance of credit markets in how Americans cope and get by in the contemporary economy. As the emergence of buy now pay later instruments illustrate, financial markets continue to innovate in ways that both provide opportunities for liquidity but also pose challenges in repayment. We see our work as aiding social science of inequality, poverty, and mobility to do better to keep up with the speed and innovation in financial markets.

abstractText:
Demand for high-performance permanent magnets is increasing rapidly for applications such as wind turbine generators and electric and hybrid car motors. Samarium-cobalt (Sm-Co) and Neodymium-iron-boron (Nd-Fe-B) rare earth magnets are generally used for such challenging applications. While rare earth magnets are the best currently available permanent magnets, they tend to be brittle, suffer from thermal shock and experience corrosion. Additionally, rare earth mining has been associated with severe environmental degradation and prohibitive energy usage. Nickel-iron, which has been identified in meteorites as the compound Tetrataenite where it transformed from a high temperature phase to a low temperature magnetic phase over thousands of years, has magnetic properties comparable to that of rare earth magnets. This award develops nickel-iron based permanent magnets using quantum-mechanical calculations to predict the effects of alloying and experiments to verify the effects of these additional elements on the transformation kinetics and magnetic properties of these materials. A novel pulsed electrical heating is used to accelerate the phase transformation. The development of novel nickel-iron magnets enables production of permanent magnets at low cost, which impacts the U.S. economy and security. The project engages women and under-represented minorities in multi-disciplinary research activities and develops a website that offers simple virtual experiments to explain to a wide audience magnetism and the materials science of permanent magnets.

The L10-structured compound nickel-iron (NiFe) has the potential to replace rare earth (RE) magnets at low cost. NiFe has a magnetic anisotropy energy, ku, of 1.3 x 106 J.m-3 and a saturation magnetization m0MS of 1.59 Tesla, which is comparable to that of Nd2Fe14B, and it has good corrosion resistance. The challenge is that the binary L10 compound has a very low transformation temperature from the high-temperature face centered cubic (f.c.c.) phase of about 320oC that forms on casting and, thus, orders very slowly at temperatures where it is stable. This project combines ab initio quantum mechanical calculations and experimental work to design new L10-structured NiFe magnets with ternary elemental additions. These ternary compounds potentially have a significantly higher f.c.c.-to-L10 transformation temperatures and higher diffusivities than binary NiFe but have similar saturation magnetizations. Thus, the L10 phase can be produced at higher temperature in short, commercially-viable times utilizing electro-pulse annealing of cold-worked material, which has also been shown to dramatically accelerate recrystallization in NiFe. Commercially, NiFe can be manufactured by continuous electro-pulse annealing of rolls of sheet material or of rods and, being ductile, can easily be machined into various shapes.

projectOutComesReport:
Demand for high-performance permanent magnets has been increasing rapidly for important energy applications such as wind turbine generators and motors in both electric and hybrid cars. Rare earth (RE) magnets serve most of this market. However, there are significant societal issues with RE magnets, i.e., over 95% of REs are produced in China with the possibility of restrictions on exports; there has been substantial price volatility of RE elements; RE mining has been associated with severe environmental degradation, particularly in China, because of the low-grade ores that require large amounts of both water and energy to process. The high cost of RE magnets is largely because of the large water and energy usage in the refining process. Thus, there is a clear need for low-cost, more-environmentally-friendly permanent magnets that could replace RE magnets. A possible RE magnet replacement is NiFe, which has theoretical magnetic properties comparable to RE magnets and is much lower cost. Thus, being able to produce NiFe magnets would be a paradigm shift in magnet usage for the energy-related applications.

The goal of this project was to produce a cost-effective alternative to high-performance RE permanent magnets through developing NiFe magnets. The main issue with NiFe is that the disorder-to-order transition temperature from the high-temperature, face-centered-cubic crystal structured phase to the low-temperature, permanent magnet, tetragonal crystal structured phase is very low at around 320oC. This means that it is very difficult to get the transformation to occur in reasonable timescales. This project aimed to raise the order-disorder transition temperature, increase the diffusion kinetics, or develop a novel processing route that accelerates the phase transformation so that atomic ordering can occur at a reasonable rate.

Ternary elemental additions were investigated as the primary strategy to either raise the order-disorder transition temperature or increase the diffusion kinetics. Quantum-mechanical computational methods were employed to identify promising elements and compositions for experimental analysis, thus avoiding the time consuming and labor-intensive iterative trial-and-error involved in conventional experimental materials design. Several elements were identified that could potentially raise the transformation temperature. However, this depended on whether the ternary element was used to replace the nickel or the iron. Elements that were predicted to increase the transformation temperature when the iron was replaced are Mo, W, Re, V, Bi, Sn, Te. Many elements lowered the transformation temperature. When a ternary elemental addition was used to replace nickel, most elements lowered the transformation temperature. Only phosphorus, arsenic and iridium were predicted to show much increase in the transformation temperature when used to replace 1 atomic percent nickel. Based on these predictions, a number of alloys were cast with elemental additions such as Mo or Sn, but no effect on producing the low temperature phase was found.

Another strategy for shortening the timescales required to manufacture tetragonal NiFe was to investigate experimentally the electropulse annealing of cold-rolled material. Electropulse annealing uses very large currents (several hundred amps) to heat the material. To reach the targeted temperature, the current is rapidly turned on and off with durations for each pulse of the order of a few microseconds. This novel methodology was shown to dramatically accelerate recrystallization in NiFe. However, it did not lead to the formation of the low-temperature tetragonal phase.

Other routes to producing the low temperature tetragonal phase were also explored. One route was to make carbon-doped material that can be transformed to a martensitic phase by quenching from high temperature and then heated to produce the tetragonal phase. Another route that explored was mechanical cryomilling to produce a nanostructured material, which can then be heated and transformed to the tetragonal phase.

The project supported a PhD student, a master’s student and seven undergraduates. Both the PhD student and the master’s student were trained in casting alloys, processing them by cold rolling and electropulse annealing and analyzing the resulting materials using x-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy. The undergraduates learnt how to cast alloys and analyze them using x-ray diffraction. Some undergraduates undertook the electropulse annealing while others undertook the cryomilling approach or the martensitic transformation approach. Results were published in journals and presented at conferences.

abstractText:
Computer Science is a rapidly growing field leading to new kinds of computational problems. For example, data is being produced at a huge rate today, and an algorithm's access to it is restricted either due to sheer volume or due to ownership concerns. This forces designers to revisit classical algorithms. In machine learning, one uses clustering algorithms to learn about unlabeled data. However, the presence of noise and anomalies can distort this, and one needs good outlier-detection algorithms. The goal of this project is to use and enhance techniques from mathematical optimization to tackle these new algorithmic challenges. In doing so, the project will create unified methodologies to attack problems arising in different areas. In turn, these news ideas will also lead to answers to classical optimization problems. Work on this project will go hand-in-hand with the creation of relevant courses in undergraduate and graduate curriculum which focus on these new algorithmic insights. The educational component of this project also includes a plan for injecting computer science and algorithmic thinking into the K-12 system.
 
In more detail, the project focusses on three areas. The first area is about query access models where algorithms can access data only via asking certain kinds of questions.  A main thrust is to completely understand the query complexity of fundamental problems such as submodular function optimization and matroid intersection.  The second area is the development of new approximation-algorithm techniques to tackle outlier-detection problems in clustering. The project will also focus on richer objective classes for clustering, thereby paving the way for integer convex optimization. The third area is the development of the primal-dual optimization schema to design faster parallel algorithms, especially for perfect matchings in graphs, which is a fundamental problem in algorithms. By addressing these questions, this project will create new algorithmic paradigms that will be useful for tackling a range of modern-day relevant problems.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project addresses the need for rapid, accurate, and high-throughput diagnostic testing platforms. Given the urgency of this need, the team's first product aims to support ongoing SARS-CoV-2 disease diagnosis by enabling point-of-care diagnosis from a patient nasal swab within minutes. Despite the prevalence and rapid spread of the disease, the majority of diagnostic tests remain time intensive, require numerous external reagents, and/or lack detection sensitivity in the early stages of infection. The team hypothesizes that the technology has significant value in this space and is interested in exploring this potential value more thoroughly through I-Corps. The technology may also find application to other diagnostic markets that traditionally rely on culture-based detection and/or nucleic acid amplification technologies. The platform can process complex biofluids and large volume samples, which could translate to pathogen detection in a range of biological fluids, including urine, saliva, and synovial fluid for the detection of urinary tract infections, respiratory infections, and joint infections, respectively. There are also a number of potential non-medical applications, including food and water quality monitoring, biosecurity surveillance, and applications to the point-of-care.

This I-Corps project focuses on understanding the market need for the platform, which performs nanoscale Pathogen Enrichment and Detection (nano-PED). For infectious disease, current diagnostic methodologies remain extremely time-consuming, costly, and rely on labor intensive sample preparation steps, followed by additional steps for pathogen identification and characterization.  The platform aims to: 1) circumvent laborious sample preparation steps through direct isolation of rare pathogens from a patient's biofluid sample, and 2) eliminate the need for molecular amplification through ultrasensitive, sequence-specific nucleic acid detection. More specifically, nano-PED capitalizes on the diverse scientific applications of nanoparticles to integrate pathogen capture and species-specific detection onto a single chip. The technology is a micro-scale platform that isolates bacteria, fungi, and/or virus from a patient sample and identifies the disease-causing pathogen through ultrasensitive nucleic acid characterization.

projectOutComesReport:
The team met at Dartmouth college during their time as Ph.D. Innovation Fellows, where they developed the underlying components of a technology that can sense DNAs and RNAs from complex patient samples. The team initially participated in the Dartmouth I-Corps Site Grant, where they spoke to over 30 local stakeholders to guage applicability ot their platform to a range of clinical settings. With this initial traction, the team looked to validate some of these findings in a larger cohort of stakeholders. The goal of this I-Corps project was to conduct customer discovery with stakeholders to identify a market need for this technology (and first potential clinical indication) and map out a potential business model.

The team started with the hypothesis that COVID-19 or hospital infections would be an ideal beachhead market due to perceived public desire for a better solution than existing solutions. After about 20 interviews, the team learned that most of these entities already have high-throughput screening methods, and thus did not express the desire for a better solution. This led the team to the outpatient women’s health space, where they conducted they final 60 interviews of the 7 week program. After the on-site portion of the program, the team continued engagement with stakeholders through attendance at 3+ academic conferences and trade shows. 

The project directly supported a young team of two women looking to understand a potential market need for a technology that they developed. It also allowed the team to focus intentionally on the specific needs associated with traditionally underserved populations, including women and those who live in rural areas of the US and globally. 

As a result of this work, the team spun out the technology, sourced laboratory space, and conducted pilot clinical studies in collaboration with New England's leading hospitals. Concrete achievements from this grant include a executed licensing agreement, a successful NSF SBIR Phase I award (January 2022) as well as an oversubscribed, venture-backed Series A financing (August 2022).

abstractText:
In understanding the large-scale changes of the Greenland Ice Sheet, wide coverage is needed. While aircraft and satellites produce extensive elevation-change datasets, and regional climate models predict snowfall at high resolution, both systems require calibration and validation by on-the-ice means. Hence, there is a need for extensive on-ice elevation survey data in Greenland, typically collected using the Global Positioning System (GPS). Ground-based traverses have been highly successful in collecting such on-ice information. Similarly, on-ice static GPS stations have been installed for short-term glaciology projects. Both approaches, however, suffer significant drawbacks. The first is cost. Ground traverses are logistically complex and expensive. For traditional static stations, the high cost is associated with the hardware and the transport of large numbers of batteries due to the power required to run these stations through the dark winter. The second is limitations in spatial and temporal coverage.  Traverses offer excellent spatial coverage, but temporally only a single snapshot in time over the traverse route. Conversely, static stations offer excellent temporal resolution, but operate at a fixed point and thus limited spatial resolution. 

This project will create a dense network of static on-ice GPS stations in Greenland. New GPS technology allows for a reduction in costs by leveraging the newest generation of chipsets, which offer extremely low power consumption. While currently unproven for collecting science data on ice sheets, these chipsets are now integrated in the current generation of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and, when operated using Real Time Kinematic (RTK) corrections in these situations, claim centimeter-scale positioning accuracy. Over three phases, the project will 1) install a network of stations in the study area; 2) develop a standalone GNSS receiver station for deployment outside the original network; and 3) deploy a wider network of stations on the Greenland Ice Sheet. This project will also integrate research and education by supporting a graduate student who will be actively involved in all aspects of the project, and by partnering with the Women in Science Project to train a first-year female undergraduate student during a 20-week internship in each year of the project.

projectOutComesReport:
The primary motivation of this research was to enhance the accuracy and spatio-temporal coverage of ice measurements on the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS), including ice velocity, surface elevation, and snow accumulation. These measurements can all be carried out with a single technology–Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). However, traditional ground-based GNSS is limited due to the cost associated with instrumentation, high battery power requirements, and logistical constraints due to difficulty in on-ice deployments. Meanwhile, space-based measurements of ice velocity, surface elevation, and accumulation are often limited temporally, or otherwise require on-the-ground validation or calibration.

This project addressed these challenges by developing and deploying a low-power network of GNSS instruments built on open-source, cost-effective, and field-ready technology. During the first year of the project, twelve prototype instruments were set up in the vicinity of the ice divide in Greenland, near Summit Station. Due to their design, these stations were rapidly deployed by a team of three over the course of two days, and each instrument was configured to log data at weekly or bi-monthly intervals throughout the wintertime, when there is no sunlight to recharge the battery. During the second field season, a thirteenth station was deployed and configured to log data daily, providing a continuous dataset of ice velocity and snow accumulation. Each station proved capable of providing scientific quality, mm-precise data over the course of this project.

This network demonstrated that the design of the instrument met our primary requirements: (1) low cost: (<225 USD ea) relative to commercially available options, (2) low power: capable of gathering data throughout the winter without solar recharging or multiple batteries, and (3) easy to deploy: simple interface and programmable in Arduino environment, requiring <15 minutes to set up in the field. Beyond these criteria, these instruments track the most complete network of L1 and L2 (multiband) satellites across all major GNSS constellations, providing scientific-grade measurements. Details on both the instrument design and performance in this extreme environment are detailed in a publication in the Journal of Glaciology, and the hardware and software files are freely available on github.com/glaciology/ogre.

Beyond our open-source and freely available hardware, our findings were disseminated through 2+ peer-reviewed publications, 6+ conference presentations, and numerous outreach efforts. One MSc student was supported by this grant, who has continued to pursue a PhD focused on the scientific results and applications of the technology developed in this project. Now, the data from our GNSS network are available at the National Science Foundation Arctic Data Center. These data captured a high resolution snow accumulation time series, using a technique called GNSS interferometric reflectometry (GNSS-IR), which allowed us to detect a cm-level gradient in yearly accumulation between the ice divide and downslope 30 km to the west. We expanded the scope of GNSS-IR using these instruments by demonstrating their sensitivity to small-scale surface roughness, which is a difficult parameter to measure. These findings are detailed in a

publication in The Cryosphere. The ice velocity and surface elevations also derived from these instruments provide a valuable benchmark for space-based measurements. These data are being used to complement ongoing efforts to ensure the robustness and stability of NASA’s Ice, Cloud,and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2), and may also be used to benchmark space-based ice velocity estimates. We anticipate that this valuable dataset will contribute to our understanding of the dry snow zone dynamics in Greenland for years to come.

Finally, by the end of this project, our goal was to ensure that this technology would continue to have an impact. Through various partnerships, over 60 of these instruments have now been deployed collaboratively throughout Greenland, the U.S.A., and Canada, adopted by researchers studying ice dynamics and snow, along with Earth Sciences educators. Locations included hard-to-reach areas in Greenland such as the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream, Jakobshavn Isbrae, Helheim Glacier, and Raven Camp. In one instance, over ten stations were deployed on a glacier in a single day, significantly cutting costs and field time for that particular project. This project has expanded research and education infrastructure with its low-cost, open-source nature, and its adaptability means future projects can modify the instrument to their needs.

abstractText:
The Arctic sea ice cover is in decline. The areal extent of sea ice is decreasing and the ice is getting thinner. Observing and understanding this ice loss is critical to predict future ice conditions and develop plans to respond to these changes. This project uses autonomous buoys to determine the mass balance of sea ice. The sea ice mass balance is a simple concept. It is how much the ice grows in winter and how much it melts in summer; specifically, how much it melts on the surface of the ice and how much on the bottom of the ice. This separation enables the relative contributions of the atmosphere and the ocean to be determined. These buoys will be deployed at key locations in partnership with other instruments measuring conditions in the atmosphere and ocean. Buoy deployment locations are influenced by modeling studies and by logistical opportunities. The ice mass balance data will be used to gain insights into the drivers of the current rapid sea ice decline and changes in the characteristics of the upper layers of the Arctic Ocean and to improve models of sea ice and climate.

Seasonal ice mass balance buoys are based on a spar-type hull design. They are designed to be installed in the ice and to float stably upright in open water. The sensor package on the buoy provides time series data on position, barometric pressure, vertical profiles of air-snow-ice-upper ocean temperature, snow depth, ice thickness, ice growth, surface melt, bottom melt, and ocean heat flux. This project will procure and deploy a minimum of eight buoys per year; process and archive the data from these buoys to be fully, freely, and immediately accessible to all users; implement new sensors into the buoy production process and make this ever-improving technology available; and continue to post mass balance results on a publicly accessible website. The ice mass balance buoys will also be the centerpiece of a middle school science program called “Adopt-a-buoy.” By working with an observation site at the school, where they collect data similar to measurements by buoys installed in the Arctic, eighth-grade students will gain firsthand experience formulating hypotheses, accessing, processing and analyzing data, and presenting results to their peers.

abstractText:
The Arctic is warming at a rate faster than elsewhere on Earth, resulting in changes to Arctic ecosystems that may affect global climate. Permafrost is ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years. It occurs under approximately one fourth of the northern hemisphere's land surface and contain as much carbon as the entire atmosphere.  Permafrost thaw leads to changes in the dominant vegetation and makes the carbon stored in the permafrost soil vulnerable to decomposition, but existing measurements and models disagree about the implications of these changes for the global carbon cycle.  This research project investigates how processes mediated by microbes, minerals, and their interactions with vegetation affect the vulnerability of carbon in permafrost soils.  The researchers are carrying out laboratory and growth chamber studies to investigate microbial communities and the transformations of carbon with permafrost thaw. They are incorporating the results of those studies into Earth system models to understand feedbacks to the climate system. This research is addressing critical knowledge gaps about how carbon stored in frozen permafrost will affect the Earth's carbon cycle, which is information urgently needed to inform climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies.

This project is addressing the question: how will feedbacks between plants and soils (specifically minerals and microbes) affect arctic soil carbon balance in response to global change? Using state-of-the-science tools, such as microbial sequencing and stable isotope tracing, the researchers are carrying out (1) laboratory incubations to determine how soil microbial communities and mineralogy affect the fate of plant exudates and the vulnerability of native soil organic matter in thawed permafrost, and (2) plant-soil growth chamber mesocosms to trace belowground plant deposits into permafrost soils under ambient and elevated CO2. These findings are being used to develop and evaluate a microbial-enabled model that can handle the complexity of plant-microbe-mineral feedbacks. This soil model is being integrated into the Community Land Model (CLM) to predict the impact of permafrost thaw on the arctic carbon budget. This research enables better long-term projections of permafrost-climate feedbacks. The project is training the next generation of interdisciplinary Arctic scholars well-versed in scales ranging from microbial genes to global elemental cycles through PhD assistantships, postdoctoral research, and undergraduate laboratory education. In addition, the project provides training for up to 50 early career researchers on the theory and practice of land modeling, with a special focus on Arctic systems.

abstractText:
Non-technical abstract

This research will lead to new understanding of how certain very widely-used materials behave and why they sometimes misbehave. Some solid materials are crystalline; table salt and sugar are two familiar examples. In these cases the atoms or molecules that make up the solid are regularly positioned and highly organized, and their structure and properties do not change with time - they are at equilibrium.  In many other cases the solids are glassy, as if the particles in the liquid state were stuck in place. Window glass is just one example; it is made of small molecules containing silicon and oxygen.  A large fraction of specially designed materials, which often involve very large molecules known as polymers, are also in the glassy solid state.  Although glassy solids have been part of our surroundings for centuries, there are still aspects of their behavior that are not well understood. Examples from daily life include protective coatings, photoresists, polymers reinforced with nanoparticles, membranes, and filters. In each of these cases a significant fraction of the glassy solid molecules are near an interface; different kinds of experiments have led to the conclusion that these molecules can behave very differently from neighboring molecules ensconced in the bulk. A related problem is that, where glassy solid properties are carefully designed to optimize performance, as the material ages its properties can change in undesirable ways. These situations reflect the fact that glassy solids, unlike crystalline solids, are not at equilibrium; and their properties can shift over time.  These changes can affect their performance, and therefore cause problems. This project will produce new ways of modeling glassy solids that will account for the influence of a neighboring surface on how molecules pack. The models will work together with experimental data and lead to new methods for understanding and predicting the ways that glassy material behavior can change when interfaces are present.

Technical abstract

Dynamic relaxation of material begins locally through segmental motion; its progression over short time and length scales drives the longer and larger response. Dynamic behavior also reflects the local structural and energetic characteristics that determine thermodynamic properties. The research proposed here will reveal deep connections between these realms by using and advancing thermodynamic (Locally Correlated Lattice) and dynamic (Cooperative Free Volume) models originated in the PI's research group. This new set of tools will be applied to predict glassy material behavior over a wide range of conditions. Two areas of particular focus involve the presence of interfacial regions and the effect of different experimental pathways used to mimic the effects of long-time aging. This research involves interrelated projects:

(a) A  model will be developed for the interfacial region from very near (nm) the surface to distances where bulk behavior is recovered. It will lead to predictions for local density, mobility (mobile layer thickness), segmental relaxation times, and the changing lengthscale of cooperative motion, as functions of distance from the interface, temperature, and film thickness.

(b) A new model will be introduced for nanocomposites that reflects differences between the interfacial region (next to the particles) and the matrix. This model, informed by thermodynamic properties, will lead to predictions for segmental dynamics and changes in cooperative length scales as functions of temperature, pressure, and nanoparticle loading.

(c) Advances from (a) and (b) will lead to new ways for connecting the thermodynamic and dynamic properties of glass formers to their long term stability.  This work will also lead to insight about how those connections depend on the experimental path to glassiness.

The materials targeted by this project serve an extremely wide range of functions, and this research will lead to new insight about how their molecular nature links to the particular properties that make them uniquely suited to their applications. The new models resulting from this research will be accessible and generally useful for linking thermodynamic properties to dynamic behavior.

The PI will further successful efforts to involve and encourage STEM participation among women and will continue working with graduate and undergraduate students to add new resources on polymer-related science to the public knowledge base. The PI will also continue energetic efforts to introduce fundamental concepts in physical science to the general public.

projectOutComesReport:
The research supported through this award has led to models for understanding and predicting the properties and behavior of solid materials having a glassy (amorphous) structure.  One category of study was glassy thin films, which play key roles in electronics, optics, membranes, coatings, and many other applications. The other was nanocomposites, which are made up of a polymer matrix plus small (i.e. nanometer sized) particles (e.g. silica) dispersed throughout. The particular components can be chosen to meet high performance needs, for example in structural materials that appear in products ranging  from home goods to energy storage to space exploration. A feature shared by all the materials studied is the existence of a large “interfacial” region.  In a nanocomposite this is the area at the surface of the nanoparticles, while in a film it is the region where the material meets air or a solid substrate. Understanding the influence of these regions is key in controlling material properties.

The approach involved simple theoretical and computational models developed in our group. The computational approach is the Limited Mobility (LM) model; it simulates how molten material transitions to a glassy solid. Our LM work led to predictions about  important characteristics and behavior of nanocomposites, successfully capturing effects of different kinds of nanoparticles on the change from melt to glass upon cooling, which happens at the ‘glass transition temperature’, Tg. Turning to analytic modeling, we have created two theories: The Locally Correlated Lattice (LCL) is a fundamental theory  in the area of  thermodynamics; it describes material behavior as pressure, temperature, volume, and composition, are changed.  The Cooperative Free Volume (CFV) theory describes a particular dynamic process such that a molecular segment of a material makes a local hop a distance of about its own size, enabled by some of its neighbors cooperatively moving slightly out of the way. This occurs as part of what is called dynamic ‘relaxation’, whereby a material finds a nondestructive way to dissipate added energy. Since the ability to carry out a segmental hop depends on available space nearby, the presence of an open interface, or of an impenetrable surface (e.g. from a nanoparticle or a substrate) may affect the rate at which this move is successful.

Our nanoparticle studies made use of all approaches described above. The simulation experiments showed that the presence of even completely inert nanoparticles interferes with Tg, and also revealed trends in how changing the particle concentration and the matrix-particle interaction could shift Tg. The simulation results were in strong agreement with  experimental data, and illustrated this fundamental property of a nanocomposite can be ‘tuned’ by choice of polymer, nanoparticle type, and composition. The theoretical studies explained some puzzling experimental data, showing how addition of nanoparticles could indeed lower the density of a composite, yet still not increase the space available for hops, and therefore leave  the segmental dynamics unchanged.

Another series of studies focused on predicting how the presence of interfaces changes local dynamics and the glass transition in glassy materials. A key idea is that knowing the unoccupied, or ‘free’, volume (V-f) in a sample is very revealing. This plus the volume occupied (V-occ) by all of the atoms add together to make up the total volume, V. We showed how V-f can be unambiguously determined from experiment, and revealed links between this quantity and a variety of properties and behavior. For example, our work has led to predictions for changes in segment mobility and sample Tg with film thickness that were subsequently verified by experimentalists. Our studies have also demonstrated that the effects of a free interface are equivalent to the effects of changing the external pressure. Pressure is a very important facet of processing glassy materials into useable objects. So, for example, we can predict how much additional external pressure to apply to an ultrathin film in order to recover dynamics that match a bulk sample at atmospheric pressure. Further, we can make predictions about film behavior using the more readily available data on bulk samples, alone, without needing any experimental data on the films. These studies have demonstrated that using our LCL and CFV models together lead to powerful new insights about materials. 

Alongside these scientific advances, NSF support has enabled us to have a broad impact in the larger scientific and learning communities. The former is related to the applicability of our tools to a range of problems extending well outside our own areas of immediate interest. The latter has been ongoing through the engagement of students at all levels – from undergraduate through post-doctoral – in this work, with an especially strong record of involving women. Further, as the Dean of Science, the PI has been very active in growing and strengthening her academic scientific community.

abstractText:
Life originates in water.  Most embryos develop in fluids with buoyancy, a force that only exists when there is gravity. Many species are pseudo-symmetric, and as such, breaking the left-right symmetry is essential for proper development. For example, axial rotation occurs in the development of many mammals and birds, and is one of the earliest developmental events that breaks the left-right symmetry. During axial rotation, the embryonic brain undergoes rotation to correctly place the organs.  If it fails to do this correctly, significant birth defects can result. The research goal of this award is to understand how body forces such as gravity and buoyancy affect embryonic development and symmetry breaking. The project will examine how the absence of buoyancy and gravity change the growth and brain torsion in chicken embryos in experiments to be conducted on the International Space Station. These experiments, together with computational simulations, will be employed to identify the key mechanical factors driving axial rotation. The research results will be incorporated into solid mechanics and biomechanics courses, and the development of high school and undergraduate research experiences. Computational models will be made available on a website, and videos of this research will be uploaded to YouTube. An annual workshop will be held to host visitors and share scientific knowledge. The results of this work will benefit life on earth by increasing our understanding of embryonic development, which may lead to new ways to prevent birth defects.
 
This research combines embryo experiments in space with computational modeling to identify the regulative role of physical forces in the early development. The team will study how changes in buoyancy and gravity can affect the growth of brain and heart, and how the development of brain and heart are interdependent during the process of embryonic brain torsion, an important symmetry-breaking event that is essential for establishing the correct body plan. Physical forces drive and regulate the twisting of the brain. Thus, the idea that brain torsion not only depends on body curvature (flexure) and the forces exerted by the vitelline membrane, but is also a result of heart development and body forces such as gravity and buoyancy will be explored. The hypothesis that buoyancy helps the heart and brain tube maintain the right morphology, and that the disturbance in buoyancy or heart development will be detrimental for symmetry breaking and embryonic development will be tested. The work will unveil new mechanical aspects of morphogenesis and develop new models for embryonic development that take into account the effects of body forces. Insights gained from this work will enhance our understanding of mechanics of embryogenesis, particularly the development of left-right asymmetry.

abstractText:
Communication is central to modern computing systems, which involve data distributed across multiple entities. Developing communication-efficient algorithmic strategies (protocols) to solve problems featuring distributed data is therefore an important practical goal. Correspondingly, communication complexity---which studies the possibilities and limitations of such protocols---is important to foundational research in computer science.  In fact, the influence of communication complexity runs much deeper, because the operation of an algorithm can itself be seen as a careful orchestration of information flow from input bits to output bits, which gives rise to a communication protocol between abstract entities. Key questions in communication complexity are: how much efficiency is gained by allowing the communicating parties to (a) use randomized strategies that may err with some small probability, or (b) use a complex pattern of interactive communication as opposed to a simple one?  This project will address some such questions, seeking theorems that provably require fresh mathematical ideas, forcing an expansion of our mathematical arsenal. The project aims to grow the foundations of communication complexity either through novel lower bounds or by obtaining surprising new protocols that may teach us algorithmic lessons.

Viewing communication as information flow and quantifying this using the machinery of Shannon entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence is a powerful technique for proving lower bounds on the communication required to accomplish a task. This project's central goal is to make progress on problems where this general paradigm provably cannot work. The investigator has identified some concrete communication tasks where a deterministic solution plausibly requires considerably more resources than a randomized solution, and proposes to prove such separations by developing a more delicate quantification of information flow that is attuned to deterministic communication protocols. Additionally, the project will study a class of communication problems involving parties with asymmetric knowledge (the so-called Arthur-Merlin setting, where one super-player knows all of the distributed input but is not blindly trusted by the other, regular, players), where classical information theory fails to capture the communication from the super-player.

projectOutComesReport:
This research project sought to quantify the communication or space resources required for solving basic algorithmic problems involving large amounts of input data spread across two or more "players" working cooperatively. Such problems arise when proving mathematical theorems about the inherent limitations of many aspects of computing. In this project, the most important aspect was to understand streaming computation, which calls for processing a continuous flow of information. Imagine trying to make sense of a fast-moving river of information where decisions need to be made quickly based on what arrives, without the luxury of pausing to sort through everything.


During this project, the PI and his collaborators established several hardness results related to these problems. Additionally, the PI and collaborators designed new and more efficient algorithms for certain data streaming challenges. A key highlight of the project was the development of a well-rounded theory for streaming algorithms that function effectively despite adversarial feedback-loop effects caused by outputs influencing future inputs processed by the same algorithm. This theory provides insights into both the possibilities and limitations in the realm of data streaming and distributed computing, based on results published throughout the project.

In addition to advancing research, this project played a crucial role in establishing a new course at Dartmouth focused on Information Theory for Computer Science. Given that Dartmouth does not have a traditional electrical engineering department, this course fills an important gap, providing students with essential knowledge and skills in this vital area of study. By equipping the next generation of computer scientists with knowledge rooted in advanced research, this initiative will help shape the future of computing and its diverse applications.
